items.title: Sudan: Site Profile - Tawila Camp: North Darfur Humanitarian Response (15 November, 2026)
items.author: Norwegian Refugee Council
items.content:
Country: Sudan
Source: Norwegian Refugee Council

Please refer to the attached Infographic.

Operational Context & Approach

Since September 2026, Tawila has experienced successive waves of displacement, primarily from areas around Al Fasher, driven by severe food and resource shortages following poor rainfall, compounded by farmer–nomad tensions. As of 12 November 2026, 3,441 newly arrived HHs had been recorded. Arrivals initially concentrated in the Camp A - expansion area (Al-Omda, Abnagour), adding pressure to overstretched services. Phased relocations to Tina began on 17 October 2026; 3,044 HHs from the recent displacement wave were reported to have relocated. These arrivals are tracked separately from the population baseline of the five established camps.

Displacement continues across multiple locations. In Sharq Rwanda, the 1–2 November assessment identified 315 newly displaced HHs (1,585 people), with later operational updates indicating around 900 HHs. Tarni/Ajaj remains a proposed relocation area.

Reception capacity, shelter, food, water, sanitation, health and protection needs remain acute for newly arrived and relocated families, alongside unmet needs in the established camps.

While acknowledging the broader displacement situation and ongoing new arrivals, this Site Profile focuses on the five largest camps in Tawila, covering their population, service availability and priority needs and gaps.

items.title: Syria: Explosive Ordnance Knowledge, Attitudes and Practices survey in Aleppo governorate - Analysis and recommendations for Risk Education
items.author: HAMAP Humanitaire
items.content:
Country: Syrian Arab Republic
Source: HAMAP Humanitaire

Please refer to the attached file.

Executive summary

Safe Land and HAMAP-Humanitaire conducted this Knowledge, Attitudes and Practices (KAP) survey to better understand how communities in Aleppo Governorate perceive and respond to the threat of explosive ordnance (EO), and to ensure that future Explosive Ordnance Risk Education (EORE) activities are evidence-based and adapted to local realities. Data collection took place across eight target locations: Castello, Youth Housing, Khan Al-Asal, Maqbala, Al-Rashedin, Al-Mallah, Haritan and Ratyan.

Findings confirm that EO contamination remains a major humanitarian and socio-economic challenge in Aleppo. 82% of respondents reported avoiding certain areas because of EO hazards, while 62% had personally seen or encountered an explosive device and 74% knew someone who had been injured or killed by EO. Exposure is particularly acute in agricultural areas, where contamination continues to restrict access to farmland, grazing land and livelihoods.

Although awareness of contamination is widespread, important knowledge and behaviour gaps persist. While 91% of respondents had heard about mines or explosive remnants of war in their area, only 49% reported being able to identify a suspicious item, with significant disparities between men (63%) and women (33%). Unsafe reactions remain common: 1/3 of respondents would ignore a suspicious object, 15% reported they would handle or move it, and only 32% would report it to the authorities. In the event of an EO accident, most respondents would rush directly to assist the victim, potentially exposing themselves to secondary hazards.

The survey revealed a strong demand for risk education. 94% of respondents considered EORE important, while local NGOs (58%) and national authorities (52%) were identified as the most trusted actors to deliver awareness activities. Schools emerged as the preferred awareness channel, followed by community workshops, door-to-door outreach and digital platforms. Based on the findings, Maqbala, Al-Mallah and Youth Housing should be prioritised for future EORE interventions. Particular attention should be given to adult men aged 31-50, who display some of the highest levels of risky behaviour, and to adult women who demonstrated a lack of knowledge compared to men; while maintaining targeted outreach for children, adolescents, returnees and farming communities. Expanding school-based programming, strengthening digital outreach through WhatsApp and Facebook, increasing community and household engagement, and mobilising religious and community leaders will be critical to reducing EO-related risks and supporting safe recovery in Aleppo Governorate.

This KAP survey report was done jointly by Safe Land organisation and HAMAP-Humanitaire, with the special contributions of Nedal Shaheen, Bérengère Lenoir and Adèle Masson. The two organisations would like to thank all enumerators for their professionalism in conducting the data collection, all participants for their engagement in the survey and contributors in the report writing.

items.title: World: Reporting Sexual Violence and Abuse in Conflict - October 2026
items.author: Insecurity Insight
items.content:
Countries: World, Central African Republic, Chile, Haiti, India, Kenya, Nigeria, Syrian Arab Republic, Yemen
Source: Insecurity Insight

Please refer to the attached file.

This News Brief bears testimony to the brave survivors who speak about sexual violence by state bodies or conflict actors. Most events of violence are never reported. This compilation is neither complete nor representative of the extent or nature of sexual violence in general. It brings together dispersed accounts about survivors from around the world who broke the silence. Help support our work by sharing this resource with your networks. Please copy and paste this link: https://bit.ly/Oct2026SV

Past editions: September; August; July; June; May; April; March; February; January; December: November; All

Please get in touch if you are interested in curated datasets, if you have made a public statement that you would like us to include in this News Brief, to report an incident or if you have additional information on an incident we have reported on. Visit our website, join our mailing list.

Reporting Sexual Violence
By state bodies or conflict actors that particularly targets IDPs and refugees, aid, health workers or educators or students among others.

Africa
Central African Republic
01 October 2026: In Bar village, Zemio sub prefecture, Haut-Mbomou prefecture, an unspecified number of women and girls were taken away and sexually assaulted by Wagner Group and their auxiliaries, the "Black Russians' during the evening and throughout the night. The perpetrators had stormed the village in the early hours of the morning, beating and injuring some civilians. Source: Corbeau News

Kenya
09 October 2026: In Imenti Central sub-county, Meru county, a three-and-a-half-year-old girl was sexually assaulted by suspected police officers at the Kinjo Police Patrol Base. Following the attack, the child was taken to Nairobi Women’s Hospital in Meru where doctors conducted a medical examination. On 11 November, two officers were taken into custody. Source: People Daily

Nigeria
As reported on 08 October 2026: In an undisclosed location in Kaduna state, a woman was reportedly sexually abused by a Kaduna militia after they reportedly abducted her to facilitate a ransom demand for the release of a suspect arrested by police forces. The victim was killed after they collected the ransom. Source: Punch NG

Asia
India
10-11 October 2026: In Delhi city and state, three journalists were sexually harassed by police officers during a protest calling for the resignation of the country’s top election official. Source: Human Rights Watch

29 October 2026: In Saraikela-Kharsawan district, Saraikela town, Jharkhand state, a woman was raped by a police constable inside Gamharia police station after going there to seek police assistance after a dispute with her husband. The constable was arrested and five police personnel were suspended for negligence. Source: The New Indian Express

Middle East and North Africa
Syrian Arab Republic
11 October 2026: In Hama Hama governorate, a 15-year-old girl from the Alawite sect from Tal Sekkin village was sexually assaulted after being lured away in the evening by a suspected member of the General Security forces along with suspected local individuals . She was later found at the junction of Al-Hemeiri village in a critical physical and psychological condition. There were accusations of attempts to cover up the case, intimidate the girl's family and some villagers, and detain some of them. Source: SOHR

Yemen
04 October 2026: In Taiz city and governorate, a Houthi forces member was killed, stripped of clothing and had his private parts exposed, photographed and the images published by mercenaries of the Saudi-led coalition. Source: Yemen News Agency

The Americas
Chile
03 October 2026: At the Naval Maritime Garrisson, Easter Island, a 23-year-old Indigenous Rapa Nui woman was raped by at least four Marine Corps officers in the early hours of the morning during an unauthorised party. Two sergeants were later formally charged with raping the young woman. Source: Biobio Chile

Haiti
As reported on 02 October 2026: In Haiti, more than 1,000 women and girls have been raped in 2026 up until 11 September amid the gang violence crisis. Source: Africa News

As reported on 09 October 2026: In Port-au-Prince city and arrondissement, West department, 2,485 survivors of sexual violence were cared for by Doctors Without Borders (MSF) between January and May 2026, in areas affected by gang conflicts. Source: Le Nouvelliste

items.title: Humanitarian Needs and Response Trends in Northeast Nigeria, 2022-2026: A Five-Year Retrospective Analysis (November 2026)
items.author: Voices and Evidence Frontiers
items.content:
Country: Nigeria
Source: Voices and Evidence Frontiers

Please refer to the attached file.

Executive Summary

Over time, coordinated humanitarian response in Northeast Nigeria has progressed with minimal multi-year evidence and insight captured across annual datasets. This retrospective longitudinal analysis of secondary humanitarian datasets synthesizes five years of UNOCHA needs and planning datasets from 2022 to 2026 to extract actionable lessons for the future.

An examination of needs and demographic trends reveals that the crisis remains protracted, with deep vulnerabilities persisting across total People in Need (PiN). Over the five-year period, Borno consistently remained the epicenter of the crisis, while Yobe’s caseload held steady despite tighter counting boundaries in 2026. Demographically, females consistently accounted for the majority of people in need every year, while Host Communities remained the largest share of the affected population amid declining internally displaced person (IDP) and returnee proportions. Financial and operational data further demonstrates how shrinking resource envelopes reshaped the delivery architecture. A deliberate narrowing of targeting coverage became necessary as funding shrank. Simultaneously, National NGOs (NNGOs) steadily expanded their operational share to become the primary delivery backbone as International NGOs (INGOs) drew down.
Drawing on insights from the data, organizations must transition toward multi-year, cross-cutting resilience programming and diversify funding beyond traditional Humanitarian appeals. Donors and cluster leads should enforce dedicated gender-responsive funding quotas while investing in institutional capacity and direct financing for national partners. Additionally, humanitarian actors should tailor interventions to the distinct operational realities of Borno, Adamawa, and Yobe states rather than applying a uniform regional template.

items.creator: Norwegian Refugee Council
items.title: Yemen: Catastrophic civilian suffering as donors and media look elsewhere | NRC
items.author: Norwegian Refugee Council
items.content:
Country: Yemen
Source: Norwegian Refugee Council

Intensifying conflict is driving horrific levels of harm and deepening humanitarian needs across Yemen, warned Jan Egeland, Secretary General of the Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC), during a visit to the country this week.

Press release

Yemen Published 26. Nov 2026

Yemen entered this year as one of the most profound and most neglected humanitarian crises. Renewed fighting and airstrikes along multiple frontlines have uprooted hundreds of thousands of people. Despite shocking levels of suffering, the international response has withered, and conflict and civilian harm continues unabated.

In the north, home to most of the country’s population, a handful of overstretched and underfunded national and international organisations are the only remaining lifeline to millions in need. Severe funding reductions, sanctions, and the UN’s ongoing pause in its operations following detention of their aid workers have all contributed to a collapsing humanitarian response, compounded by the insecurity and access constraints.

“The situation across the country was already catastrophic, with long-term displacement and long-term humanitarian needs growing almost entirely out of sight,” said Egeland. “But now fighting has again displaced entire communities, while disrupted supply routes have driven up food and fuel prices. Across the country, families who were already struggling to survive are being pushed deeper into hunger."

Yemen’s humanitarian response faces a severe lack of funding, which can be measured by the hundreds of thousands of families who will receive no support despite being in desperate need. Just 12 per cent of funding for emergency shelter support has been received so far, drastically reducing the ability of organisations to provide any shelter support to displaced people.

“Everywhere I have been, there are people searching for food or water, children are out of school, and parents desperately worrying about how to keep their children safe. I’ve met newly displaced people forced to shelter under the leaves of banana trees propped up with sticks,” said Egeland. “I’ve seen many families receiving no aid at all, while our courageous humanitarian colleagues struggle to increase emergency relief as well as minimal services for people who have remain displaced for years.

“All parties to the conflict bear responsibility for the vast scale of harm here. All must commit, in full, to protecting civilians and facilitating a humanitarian response at the scale that Yemenis need. The powerful countries backing the armed actors must commit to making this a reality.

“Across Yemen, I’ve been meeting with NRC teams and other humanitarians who are simply desperate to do more, but conflict and access restrictions, and the lack of funding, are preventing us from meeting even the most urgent needs. The suffering caused by cruel violence in Yemen is compounded by diplomatic and funding negligence of the highest order,” said Egeland.

Notes to editors:

  • Photos from Egeland’s visit are available for free use here.
  • 321,000 people have been displaced in Yemen since the escalation broke out in August (OCHA).
  • Yemen’s 2026 humanitarian response is 23 per cent funded at 500.8 million US dollars out of 2.16 billion required (OCHA).
  • In 2023 Yemen received 1.77 billion US dollars, approximately 41% of the 4.3 billion US dollars required to assist 17.3 million people. By November 2026, only 500 million US dollars had been secured – 23% of the 2.16 billion US dollars required. This is a 72 per cent decline in funding against increasing needs (OCHA).
  • 23.1 million people across Yemen are in need of lifesaving humanitarian assistance, representing more than 65 per cent of the entire population (OCHA).
  • 18.3 million people in Yemen face food insecurity (WFP).
  • Since the escalation in August, 4,998 families have newly arrived at NRC-supported sites including 1,350 new families in Taiz, 3,130 new households in Abyan, and 518 new families in Lahj.
  • The 2026 Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan aimed, before the escalation, to reach a much-reduced target of 12 million people, even while 22 million people require assistance(HNRP). Just 16 per cent of the funding required to support food security has been received, 22 per cent for WASH, and just 12 per cent for shelter, substantially limiting assistance to vulnerable communities (OCHA).
  • Yemen featured 4th on NRC’s annual list of the world’s most neglected displacement crises this year (NRC).
  • NRC supports 25 displacement sites for internally displaced persons (IDPs) in governorates hosting people fleeing the current fighting in Taiz governorate and the West Coast.

For more information and to arrange interviews:

  • NRC global media hotline, media@nrc.no, +47 905 62 329

items.title: At the border in Chad: A first step toward safety for people fleeing conflict in Sudan | IFRC
items.author: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies
items.content:
Countries: Chad, Sudan
Source: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies

Beyond the border: improving refugees and host communities living conditions

For refugees relocated to Arkoum Camp, located more than 50 kilometres from Adré, access to safe water, adequate shelter and sanitation remains critical.

To help address these needs, the Red Cross of Chad has built 100 shelters for vulnerable households, 20 latrines, and installed a borehole. To respond to growing demands, a larger borehole has also been constructed, significantly increasing access to safe water for refugees and surrounding communities.

More broadly, the Red Cross of Chad has provided life-saving assistance to more than 900,000 people affected by the Sudan crisis. This includes 250,000 people who have received health services, 120,000 people supported with shelter and essential household items, and the construction of 1,120 latrines and 250 shower facilities across refugee camps and settlement sites.

Access to safe water has also been significantly expanded, with more than 75,000 people now benefiting from clean water services, including over 57,000 refugees in Arkoum.

Increasing support needed

Across eastern Chad, Red Cross volunteers and staff continue to work on the front line of the response. Yet the scale of the crisis continues to exceed available resources.

As of September 2026, Chad was hosting approximately 1.75 million forcibly displaced people, including 1.35 million refugees - 969,000 of whom had arrived since 2023 - and 396,000 Chadian returnees.

Since then, successive waves of violence in Sudan have continued to drive entire families into displacement. Many are hosted in and around Adré, near the Sudanese border.

Through two emergency appeals, the IFRC is supporting National Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies to assist people affected by the conflict in Sudan and across neighbouring countries. The Sudan Complex Crisis emergency appeal, and a second emergency appeal to support the neighbouring countries of Sudan where displaced people have fled (Central African Republic, Chad, Egypt, Libya, South Sudan, Ethiopia), the Sudan Crisis Regional Population Movement emergency appeal.

As the conflict persists more support is needed to avoid worse outcomes.

This includes 250,000 people who have received health services, 120,000 people supported with shelter and essential household items, and the construction of 1,120 latrines and 250 shower facilities across refugee camps and settlement sites.
Access to safe water has also been significantly expanded, with more than 75,000 people now benefiting from clean water services, including over 57,000 refugees in Arkoum.
Increasing support needed
Across eastern Chad, Red Cross volunteers and staff continue to work on the front line of the response. Yet the scale of the crisis continues to exceed available resources.
As of September 2026, Chad was hosting approximately 1.75 million forcibly displaced people, including 1.35 million refugees - 969,000 of whom had arrived since 2023 - and 396,000 Chadian returnees.
Since then, successive waves of violence in Sudan have continued to drive entire families into displacement. Many are hosted in and around Adré, near the Sudanese border.
Through two emergency appeals, the IFRC is supporting National Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies to assist people affected by the conflict in Sudan and across neighbouring countries. The Sudan Complex Crisis emergency appeal, and a second emergency appeal to support the neighbouring countries of Sudan where displaced people have fled (Central African Republic, Chad, Egypt, Libya, South Sudan, Ethiopia), the Sudan Crisis Regional Population Movement emergency appeal.
As the conflict persists more support is needed to avoid worse outcomes.

items.title: A continuing crisis: Human rights concerns around Indonesia’s piecemeal flood response in Aceh [EN/ID]
items.author: Amnesty International
items.content:
Country: Indonesia
Source: Amnesty International

Please refer to the attached files.

Indonesia: One year after devastating Aceh floods, communities face renewed flood risk as recovery stalls

One year after catastrophic floods and landslides devastated Indonesia’s Aceh province, many survivors remain without adequate housing, continue to struggle to access promised support and now face renewed flood risks from this year’s rainy season, Amnesty International said in new research published today.

Amnesty’s briefing, A Continuing Crisis, found that many communities affected by the November 2025 disaster are still living with the consequences of inadequate response and recovery efforts. Many families remain in temporary shelters, damaged homes and makeshift accommodation, while reconstruction has progressed slowly and many survivors remain uncertain about what support they are entitled to receive.

“For the survivors in Aceh, this disaster did not end when the floodwaters receded. A year later, many families are still waiting for the housing and support they were promised by the Indonesian authorities,” said Montse Ferrer, Co-Regional Director at Amnesty International.

“But not only has this crisis been allowed to continue; it has the potential to get worse. The government’s unforgivably inept response to the floods of 2025 has now left people in Aceh facing another rainy season while key recovery work from the last disaster remains unfinished.”

In late November 2025, exceptionally heavy rainfall associated with Tropical Cyclone Senyar triggered floods, flash floods and landslides across Aceh and neighbouring provinces of North Sumatra and West Sumatra. The disaster affected 53 districts and cities, killed 1,204 people and displaced more than 880,000.

“I have lived through four crises – the Aceh conflict, the tsunami, Covid and these floods. Out of them all, I feel this is the worst.”

A flood-affected resident of Aceh

Amnesty International researchers visited more than 40 villages and spoke to 35 people across three of the worst-affected regencies in Aceh and found widespread evidence that reconstruction and mitigation for future floods remains incomplete. Researchers observed damaged homes, destroyed agricultural land, unrepaired infrastructure and communities continuing to rely on temporary water sources.

One affected resident told Ammesty: “I have lived through four crises – the Aceh conflict, the tsunami, Covid and these floods. Out of them all, I feel this is the worst.”

Permanent housing remains out of reach

Indonesia’s government announced multibillion-dollar plans for rehabilitation and reconstruction across the affected provinces. Yet official figures show that only 649 of the 34,777 permanent homes required in Aceh had been completed by September 2026.

Across the villages visited by researchers, Amnesty International did not encounter a single family whose replacement home had been completed. Many survivors remained in temporary housing or accommodation provided by relatives and friends. Most had no information about when permanent housing would become available.

In more than 15 temporary housing sites visited by Amnesty International, researchers found problems including chronic overcrowding, inadequate access to clean water, damaged or unusable toilets, poor lighting, and shelters that became dangerously hot during the day.

In one settlement, families of five or six people were each living in single-room structures made from tarpaulin, timber and corrugated metal sheeting. Residents reported that entire families, including teenage children, were forced to share a single room and rainwater often entered their homes.

One woman told Amnesty International that conditions in temporary accommodation had forced her son, who has multiple disabilities, to live separately from the family because the shelter and sanitation facilities were too hard to access for him.

Communities left vulnerable as flooding returns

Amnesty International’s research also raises concerns about failures during the emergency response itself. Survivors described receiving little or no warning before floods and landslides struck, while others said communities were forced to rely on volunteers, neighbours and social media rather than official channels during the critical early days of the disaster.

One woman from Langkahan district said: “The water level was not rising despite the rain, so I thought it was going to be OK. But then, all of a sudden, we had the flood. Water was flowing in from four sides and very quickly there was water up to the window of my house.”

With little evidence that Indonesian authorities have improved flood-response capabilities over the past year, the return of heavy rains was a particular cause of anxiety. According to information reviewed by Amnesty International, dozens of floods were recorded in Aceh between April and October 2026, while flooding again affected thousands in November 2026.

These concerns are exacerbated by severe budget cuts currently affecting disaster-management authorities, which are hampering recovery and flood-mitigation efforts, along with allegations that disaster-management funds have been misused at both the local and national level. Amnesty is calling on the government to ensure that any corruption or mismanagement linked to disaster response and recovery is fully investigated and those responsible held to account.

“As Aceh faces another rainy season, it is deeply concerning that many people remain in inadequate temporary accommodation while the work needed to reduce future flood risks remains incomplete,” said Malavika Vartak, Amnesty International’s Researcher on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights.

“The authorities must urgently accelerate the delivery of adequate permanent housing, ensure survivors receive the assistance they are entitled to and strengthen measures to protect communities from future disasters.”

Background

Amnesty International conducted research between July and October 2026, including visits to more than 40 villages in Pidie Jaya, Aceh Tengah and Aceh Utara. Researchers interviewed affected residents, community activists, volunteers and civil society organizations, and visited temporary housing sites and disaster-affected communities across Aceh.

items.title: WHO Director-General's opening remarks at joint media briefing with the Ministry of Public Health, Haiti – 25 November 2026
items.author: World Health Organization
items.content:
Country: Haiti
Source: World Health Organization

Minister Sinal, Minister Forbin,

Members of the ambassadors, my colleagues from the UN, press, and friends,

Good afternoon, and thank you for joining us today.

First, I would like to sincerely thank Minister Sinal and the Government of Haiti for their warm welcome and for the constructive discussions we have had during my visit.

It has given me the chance to reaffirm WHO/PAHO's solidarity with Haiti and its people, including my personal commitment for WHO to do all in its power to support the country.

During my visit earlier today to Hôpital Universitaire La Paix here in the capital, Port-au-Prince, I saw first-hand the strain the facility and its staff are working under, and the patients and families waiting for care. It moved me.

Haiti's health system is under serious strain from the high volume of patients and the influx of trauma cases.

Armed violence, widespread displacement and disease outbreaks add to the pressure on an already fragile system.

In 2026, an estimated 4.9 million people need health assistance. Behind every number is a mother, a child, a family.

Health facilities have been forced to close, and too many families are unable to access even the most basic health services.

As you know, H.U.P. is the last major public referral hospital still operating in Port-au-Prince, a city where only 38% of health facilities are fully functional.

Across Haiti, a country of more than 11 million people, only a quarter (24.5%) of health facilities are fully functioning.

Since January of this year, with support from WHO/PAHO, H.U.P. has managed to treat more than 19 575 emergency patients, including 291 victims of gunshot wounds, perform 3086 surgeries, and handle 1442 high-risk deliveries.

From my heart, I thank the brave, committed and talented health workers who provide a lifeline for the people of Port-au-Prince.

They are working day and night in one of the most challenging humanitarian and health crises globally, and they continue to show great courage and dedication. I was proud to meet some of them earlier today.

I also want to recognize the leadership of Minister Sinal and the Ministry of Public Health and Population in sustaining essential health services under difficult circumstances.

Earlier today, I met with the Prime Minister. I left that meeting encouraged and inspired by what the government is doing with the limited resources it has, especially with maternal and child health at the center. His message to the international community was, I quote: “We will do our best, and you support us based on the priorities we set for our country.” It is a message we should listen to.

Through our Regional Office for the Americas, PAHO, WHO is working closely with the Ministry and our partners to support emergency medical care, respond to outbreaks, strengthen disease surveillance and immunization, and maintain access to essential medicines and medical supplies.

Even so, Haiti’s Ministry of Public Health and Population has moved forward with the introduction of the human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine to help prevent cervical cancer.

Our discussions have reaffirmed three shared priorities.

First, protecting health workers, patients and health facilities.

Second, ensuring safe and sustained access to essential health services.

And third, strengthening Haiti's health system to respond not only to today's emergencies, but also to tomorrow's challenges.

Health is not only a humanitarian priority.

Health is a fundamental human right, and a foundation for peace, stability and sustainable development.

These efforts require strong national leadership, sustained international solidarity and predictable financing.

I want to thank our partners for their continued support, which is helping to save lives every day.

But the needs remain significant.

The people of Haiti need our support today, and our partnership in the years ahead. They are not alone.

Minister Sinal,

You can count on WHO and PAHO's continued solidarity, commitment and support. I can say this on behalf of the whole UN family. We stand with you, and with the people of Haiti.

Thank you. Merci. Mèsi anpil.

Synopsis (short abstract)

This emergency agriculture support brief presents the results of the Data in Emergencies Monitoring (DIEM-Monitoring) survey conducted in Chad in July and August 2026. Data analysis estimated that 67 131 resident agricultural households (447 012 people) required emergency food security assistance in the six provinces covered by the survey. This brief provides humanitarian actors with a detailed analysis of the needs of agricultural households to better target interventions aimed at supporting their livelihoods, strengthening their resilience to future shocks and safeguarding the food security of rural populations.The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) established DIEM-Monitoring in June 2020. DIEM enumerators collect data several times a year across food-insecure countries, through computer-assisted telephone interviews and face-to-face surveys. These data cover shocks, agricultural livelihoods, food security and household needs, and are regularly updated and easily accessible on the DIEM Hub. DIEM products consist of dashboards, maps, briefs and aggregated data, enabling partners and stakeholders to activate mitigation measures and target vulnerable households.

items.author: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations
items.content:
Country: occupied Palestinian territory
Source: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations

Please refer to the attached file.

• By mid-2026, conditional cash+ assistance from the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) had enabled 1 700 farming households in the Gaza Strip to produce enough fresh vegetables to meet the annual vegetable intake requirements of an estimated 121 000 people, based on the dietary recommendations of FAO and the World Health Organization.1 Restoring full access to agricultural inputs could increase this figure to an estimated 284 000 people.

• Conditional cash+ assistance provided by FAO to livestock-keeping households in the Gaza Strip contributed to increases in the sheep (33 percent) and goat (8 percent) populations between November 2025 and May 2026, the first recorded increase since October 2023.2 However, the sheep and goat populations remain at approximately one-quarter and one-third of pre‑conflict levels, respectively.

• With improved security and access following the October 2025 ceasefire, FAO has distributed approximately 430 tonnes of animal feed per month, about four times the monthly volume distributed before the ceasefire.

• An FAO analysis found that every USD 1 invested in livestock protection in the Gaza Strip during 2024–2026 generated approximately USD 2.30 in livestock asset value.

items.title: DR Congo: Ituri: la MONUSCO renforce ses interventions pour protéger les civils face à la recrudescence des violences à Djugu
items.author: UN Organization Stabilization Mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo
items.content:
Country: Democratic Republic of the Congo
Source: UN Organization Stabilization Mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo

Face à la recrudescence des affrontements armés dans le territoire de Djugu, en Ituri, les Casques bleus bangladais de la MONUSCO ont mobilisé, le 22 novembre 2026, une base opérationnelle mobile afin de renforcer la protection des populations civiles dans les localités d’Akwe, de Damas et de Mbidjo, dans la région de Mongbwalu. Ce déploiement a notamment permis de faciliter, deux jours plus tard, l’évacuation de dix agents de santé engagés dans la riposte contre la maladie à virus Ebola.

Depuis plusieurs jours, la situation sécuritaire s’est fortement détériorée dans plusieurs localités du territoire de Djugu, notamment à Fataki, Bule et Gina, où des affrontements opposent les Forces armées de la République démocratique du Congo (FARDC) aux éléments du groupe armé Convention pour la révolution populaire (CRP). Le 18 novembre, de violents combats ont notamment été signalés aux environs de Bule et du site de déplacés de la plaine de Savo, qui accueille environ 70 000 personnes.

Ces violences ont provoqué de nouveaux déplacements de populations, y compris parmi des personnes ayant déjà fui l’insécurité. Vingt-quatre civils, dont treize femmes et trois enfants, ont notamment trouvé refuge auprès des Casques bleus de la MONUSCO à Bayoo.

En outre, les affrontements et les déplacements de populations signalés dans la zone d’Akwe, de Damas et de Mbidjo ont conduit le bataillon bangladais à déploiement rapide (BANRDB) de la MONUSCO à renforcer sa présence sur le terrain et à apporter une assistance aux personnes en difficulté, notamment aux personnels de santé.

L’intervention s’est toutefois heurtée à d’importantes contraintes logistiques. Le relief accidenté, le mauvais état des routes et la fragilité d’un pont en bois ont empêché les Casques bleus de poursuivre leur progression sur l’itinéraire initialement prévu. Ils ont alors exploré des solutions alternatives, tout en maintenant le contact avec les personnels de santé et l’équipe chargée de les accueillir, afin d’identifier un point de rencontre accessible.

Le 24 novembre, les Casques bleus ont ainsi pu rejoindre dix agents de santé, parmi lesquels un médecin et des infirmiers de l’hôpital général de référence d’Akwe. Ils les ont escortés jusqu’à l’hôpital de Mongbwalu, puis jusqu’à l’aire d’atterrissage des hélicoptères, en vue de leur évacuation par voie aérienne vers Bunia.

Engagés dans la riposte contre l’épidémie d’Ebola, ces agents de santé jouent un rôle essentiel auprès des populations déjà fragilisées par les violences et les déplacements. Cette intervention s’inscrit dans le cadre de l’appui de la MONUSCO aux efforts de riposte contre Ebola, notamment à travers la protection du personnel de santé et la sécurisation de l’accès aux soins pour les populations affectées par les violences.

Quatre jours plus tôt, le 20 novembre, les Casques bleus bangladais et népalais de la MONUSCO avaient facilité le retour sécurisé de 380 civils depuis Fataki jusqu’au site de déplacés de la plaine de Savo, après que des affrontements les avaient contraints à fuir. Les bénéficiaires et les autorités coutumières locales ont salué l’appui de la MONUSCO.

Dans ce contexte sécuritaire tendu, la MONUSCO a également renforcé ses patrouilles dans la zone afin de protéger les populations civiles contre les violences des groupes armés.

-Didier Vignon Dossou-Gbakon

Ces violences ont provoqué de nouveaux déplacements de populations, y compris parmi des personnes ayant déjà fui l’insécurité. Vingt-quatre civils, dont treize femmes et trois enfants, ont notamment trouvé refuge auprès des Casques bleus de la MONUSCO à Bayoo.
En outre, les affrontements et les déplacements de populations signalés dans la zone d’Akwe, de Damas et de Mbidjo ont conduit le bataillon bangladais à déploiement rapide (BANRDB) de la MONUSCO à renforcer sa présence sur le terrain et à apporter une assistance aux personnes en difficulté, notamment aux personnels de santé.
L’intervention s’est toutefois heurtée à d’importantes contraintes logistiques. Le relief accidenté, le mauvais état des routes et la fragilité d’un pont en bois ont empêché les Casques bleus de poursuivre leur progression sur l’itinéraire initialement prévu. Ils ont alors exploré des solutions alternatives, tout en maintenant le contact avec les personnels de santé et l’équipe chargée de les accueillir, afin d’identifier un point de rencontre accessible.
Le 24 novembre, les Casques bleus ont ainsi pu rejoindre dix agents de santé, parmi lesquels un médecin et des infirmiers de l’hôpital général de référence d’Akwe. Ils les ont escortés jusqu’à l’hôpital de Mongbwalu, puis jusqu’à l’aire d’atterrissage des hélicoptères, en vue de leur évacuation par voie aérienne vers Bunia.
Engagés dans la riposte contre l’épidémie d’Ebola, ces agents de santé jouent un rôle essentiel auprès des populations déjà fragilisées par les violences et les déplacements. Cette intervention s’inscrit dans le cadre de l’appui de la MONUSCO aux efforts de riposte contre Ebola, notamment à travers la protection du personnel de santé et la sécurisation de l’accès aux soins pour les populations affectées par les violences.
Quatre jours plus tôt, le 20 novembre, les Casques bleus bangladais et népalais de la MONUSCO avaient facilité le retour sécurisé de 380 civils depuis Fataki jusqu’au site de déplacés de la plaine de Savo, après que des affrontements les avaient contraints à fuir. Les bénéficiaires et les autorités coutumières locales ont salué l’appui de la MONUSCO.
Dans ce contexte sécuritaire tendu, la MONUSCO a également renforcé ses patrouilles dans la zone afin de protéger les populations civiles contre les violences des groupes armés.

items.title: DR Congo: Ituri: MONUSCO steps up interventions to protect civilians amid resurgence of violence in Djugu
items.author: UN Organization Stabilization Mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo
items.content:
Country: Democratic Republic of the Congo
Source: UN Organization Stabilization Mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo

In response to renewed armed clashes in Djugu Territory, Ituri Province, Bangladeshi peacekeepers serving with MONUSCO deployed a mobile operating base on 22 November 2026 to strengthen the protection of civilians in the localities of Akwe, Damas and Mbidjo, in the Mongbwalu area. The deployment notably helped facilitate the evacuation, two days later, of ten health workers involved in the response to the Ebola virus disease outbreak.

For several days, the security situation has deteriorated significantly in several localities across Djugu Territory, particularly in Fataki, Bule and Gina, where clashes have pitted the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (FARDC) against elements of the armed group known as the Convention for the Popular Revolution (CRP). On 18 November, heavy fighting was reported around Bule and the Savo Plain displacement site, which hosts approximately 70,000 people.

The violence has triggered further population displacement, including among people who had already fled insecurity. Twenty-four civilians, including thirteen women and three children, sought refuge with MONUSCO peacekeepers in Bayoo.

Furthermore, the clashes and population movements reported in the Akwe, Damas and Mbidjo areas prompted MONUSCO's Bangladeshi Rapid Deployment Battalion (BANRDB) to strengthen its presence on the ground and provide assistance to people in distress, particularly healthcare workers.

However, the operation faced significant logistical challenges. Difficult terrain, poor road conditions and the fragile state of a wooden bridge prevented the peacekeepers from continuing along their initially planned route. They therefore explored alternative options while maintaining contact with the healthcare workers and the team assigned to receive them, in order to identify an accessible meeting point.

On 24 November, the peacekeepers successfully reached ten healthcare workers, including a doctor and nurses from Akwe General Referral Hospital. They escorted them to Mongbwalu Hospital and then to the helicopter landing site, where they were scheduled to be evacuated by air to Bunia.

These healthcare workers, who are actively involved in the response to the Ebola outbreak, play a vital role in assisting communities already weakened by violence and displacement. This intervention is part of MONUSCO's support for Ebola response efforts, particularly through the protection of healthcare personnel and the facilitation of safe access to healthcare for populations affected by violence.

Four days earlier, on 20 November, Bangladeshi and Nepalese MONUSCO peacekeepers had facilitated the safe return of 380 civilians from Fataki to the Savo Plain displacement site after clashes had forced them to flee. The beneficiaries and local customary authorities expressed their appreciation for MONUSCO's support.

Against this backdrop of heightened insecurity, MONUSCO has also stepped up its patrols in the area to protect civilians from violence perpetrated by armed groups.

-Didier Vignon Dossou-Gbakon

items.title: Haiti: MSF teams treating alarming numbers of women for sexual violence in Port-au-Prince
items.author: Médecins Sans Frontières
items.content:
Country: Haiti
Source: Médecins Sans Frontières

Port-au-Prince – On the International Day for the Elimination of Violence Against Women, the number of victims and survivors of sexual violence seeking care at Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) facilities in Port-au-Prince, Haiti, remains alarmingly high in 2026. Most of them have been forced to flee their homes, making them particularly vulnerable. In the absence of sufficient protection services, MSF is calling on state authorities, humanitarian organisations, and civil society to urgently increase the capacity for safe shelter, strengthen referrals to healthcare, and provide sustainable support to local organisations.

Despite repeated warnings from MSF and several organisations over several years about the scale of sexual violence and its consequences for people in Port-au-Prince, the need to care for victims and survivors continues to increase in 2026. The abuse and assault of mainly women and girls are taking place in a context of armed violence, population displacement, and major difficulties for people to access healthcare and protection, particularly shelter.

Between January and October 2026, 5,635 victims and survivors were treated in MSF facilities in the city, including 804 in July alone. These figures reflect the number of people who were able to access care, particularly at the Cité Soleil hospital and the Pran Men'm clinic. However, these figures do not represent the true scale of the violence, as not all victims are able to report it systematically.

One day, two armed men burst into my home... They beat me and they both sexually assaulted me.

A survivor of sexual violence MSF treated in Port-au-Prince

“Many victims and survivors are unable to reach our facilities in time and safely,” says Marie-Camille Gauthier Lessard, project coordinator at MSF’s Pran Men'm clinic. “More than 70 per cent of the victims and survivors cared for by MSF between January and July 2026 arrived after 120 hours, a critical time limit for certain emergency medical treatments.”

In the Haitian capital, armed violence is upending the living conditions of communities, forcing many families to flee their homes to seek refuge elsewhere.

“I was living in a working-class neighbourhood with my two children. One day, two armed men burst into my home; they forced the door and came in,” says a survivor MSF treated. “They beat me and they both sexually assaulted me. Then they ordered me to leave the neighbourhood, threatening to kill me and my children if I did not go.”

“The next day, I took refuge with a friend who lived in another working-class neighbourhood. One day, while she was away, armed men broke into her house and sexually assaulted me again,” the survivor continues. “Since then, life has lost all meaning. I wanted to end my life, but someone stopped me and reminded me that I have two children to raise.”

“Today, my daughter is growing up and I realise that we are still living in this area,” she continues. “I really do not feel safe.”

One of our patients told us that she had to lie on top of her own teenage daughters to allow them to sleep, as the only way to protect them from potential assaults.

Dr Claudia Lodesani, MSF medical coordinator in Port-au-Prince

Dr Claudia Lodesani, MSF medical coordinator in Port-au-Prince, describes the situation survivors find themselves in.

“Displaced people end up in makeshift shelters such as churches, schools or stadiums, which are most of the time unsanitary and unsuitable,” says Dr Lodesani. “In these places, women and girls are particularly vulnerable. One of our patients told us that she had to lie on top of her own teenage daughters to allow them to sleep, as the only way to protect them from potential assaults.”

items.title: Bolivia Drought El Niño 2026 - DREF Operation (MDRBO023)
items.author: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies
items.content:
Country: Bolivia (Plurinational State of)
Source: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies

Please refer to the attached file.

Description of the Event

Date when the trigger was met

31-10-2026

What happened, where and when?

Bolivia is facing a severe, prolonged slow-onset drought affecting extensive areas of the Altiplano, the Inter-Andean Valleys, and El Chaco region simultaneously. Reduced rainfall, combined with above-average seasonal temperatures and the depletion of both surface and groundwater sources, has significantly impacted the availability of water for human consumption, agricultural production, livestock, and the livelihoods of thousands of rural households. The water shortage is also increasing community vulnerability to health risks, food insecurity, and temporary displacement in search of water and economic opportunities.

The situation is unfolding within a context of multiple climate-related risks. While the impacts of the drought persist, several regions of the country are also facing the likelihood of hazards associated with the 2026-2027 El Niño phenomenon, including frost, hailstorms, wildfires, flash floods, and flooding. These events could further exacerbate existing conditions and generate additional humanitarian impacts. The scale of the crisis exceeds the regular response capacities of several municipal and departmental autonomous governments, requiring the mobilization of extraordinary resources and enhanced inter-institutional coordination at the national level. Given the magnitude of the situation, the National Council for Risk Reduction and Disaster and/or Emergency Response (CONARADE) reviewed the evolution of the crisis and recommended the declaration of a national emergency through Resolution No. 014/2026, dated 30 October 2026. Consequently, the Government enacted Supreme Decree No. 5759 on 31 October 2026, activating extraordinary mechanisms for response, coordination, and resource mobilization to support emergency operations and early recovery efforts.

Throughout 2026, a progressive deterioration of water availability was observed across different regions of the country. As the dry season advanced, the impacts on water sources, crops, and livestock intensified, leading to a sustained increase in humanitarian needs.

  • Bolivian Altiplano (La Paz and Oruro Departments): Water availability for human consumption and livestock is under increasing pressure due to persistent hydrological deficits. In November 2026, water levels in Lake Titicaca at the Huatajata monitoring station were reported 0.87 m below the historical average, while key reservoirs supplying the La Paz metropolitan area were operating at relatively low storage levels, including 27.96% at Ajuankhota, 36.56% at Milluni, and 42.73% at Chacaltaya.
  • Inter-Andean Valleys (Cochabamba and Chuquisaca Departments): Below-normal rainfall conditions predominated across much of the Valleys macroregion during October 2026. According to the National Service of Meteorology and Hydrology (SENAMHI), most monitoring stations recorded fewer rainy days than normal, affecting rainfed agricultural production and increasing pressure on community water supply systems despite localized rainfall surpluses in some areas.
  • Chaco Region (Santa Cruz, Chuquisaca and Tarija): The region remains highly vulnerable due to its dependence on rainfed agriculture and livestock production and recurrent exposure to drought conditions. While rainfall conditions were mixed during October 2026, temperatures during November were forecast to reach 36-39°C across several Chaco areas, with generally limited precipitation forecast (0-10 mm) and continued exposure to conditions conducive to vegetation stress and livelihood impacts.

Situational reports from the Bolivian Red Cross indicate that the impacts vary considerably across affected departments. Water supply restrictions, agricultural losses and risks to livestock production have been reported in Chuquisaca, while Oruro has experienced significant effects on agricultural activities and camelid husbandry. In Cochabamba, particularly in municipalities of the Cono Sur region, the drying of reservoirs, lagoons and other water sources has affected both crop and livestock production. In Santa Cruz, impacts are concentrated in the Chaco region, where crop losses and pasture degradation are undermining livestock-based livelihoods. Meanwhile, in La Paz, drought conditions are occurring alongside other climate-related hazards, including heavy rainfall, hailstorms and flooding.
This diversity of impacts reflects the heterogeneous nature of the emergency and underscores the need for context-specific response measures across the affected regions.

However, due to the nationwide nature of the identified threats and the potential for simultaneous impacts associated with the 2026-2027 El Niño phenomenon, the declaration applies to the entire national territory. As a result, departments, municipalities, and communities across different regions of the country may require assistance, preparedness, and recovery interventions depending on the evolution of climatic conditions.

The declaration applies nationwide and aims to strengthen preparedness, response, and recovery, as well as to support the activation of contingency funding mechanisms. Within this context, the Bolivian Red Cross is prioritizing communities in Chuquisaca, Cochabamba, Oruro, La Paz, and Santa Cruz, based on documented needs, gaps in assistance, and the capacity of local branches.

items.author: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies
items.content:
Country: Argentina
Source: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies

Please refer to the attached file.

Description of the Event

Date of event

18-01-2026

What happened, where and when?

During the early morning of 18 January 2026, a landslide occurred in the Hermitte hill, in the city of Comodoro Rivadavia, Chubut province. The displacement of the terrain affected urban sectors located on unstable slopes, mainly in the Sismográfica, Los Tilos, El Marquesado, Mazarredo and Médanos neighbourhoods.

The phenomenon occurred in a context of accumulated rainfall and pre-existing geological conditions that favored the instability of the slopes of the Hermitte hill. It manifested as sudden, progressive movements of the ground, accompanied by the appearance of cracks, subsidence, and displacement. that caused damage to homes, streets, sidewalks, service networks and other urban infrastructures.

Country: Democratic Republic of the Congo
Source: World Health Organization

I. POINTS SAILLANTS

  • Le nombre de cas suspects de choléra notifiés à la SE45 (1 719 cas dont 31 décès, létalité de 1,8 %) est légèrement plus bas (-17,47 %) par rapport à la SE44 (2 083 cas dont 46 décès, létalité de 2,2 %).

  • La campagne de vaccination contre le choléra le long du corridor fluvial a bien démarré en Equateur et dans le Mai Ndombe. Au Sud Kivu, tout est prêt pour le début de la campagne de vaccination contre le choléra au Sud Kivu.

items.author: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations
items.content:
Country: Somalia
Source: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations

Please refer to the attached file.

Review Summary:

  • Very dry week across the country. During 17–23 November, rain was reported at only four stations: Banderbeyla (28.3 mm in 2 rainy days), Mogadishu (9.7 mm), Qansax Dheere (1.3 mm) and Cadale (0.8 mm). Satellite estimates (IMERG, 18–24 November) indicate 8–13 mm over parts of Lower Juba and less than 1 mm over the river catchments in Ethiopia.
  • Seasonal totals are almost unchanged after the dry week.
